prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock based on magic-wavelength trapping and its development to the 10^-18 regime of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single prize part for the optical lattice clock, credited to Katori and Ye. After the full round-1 exchange I think the chair's first question can be answered in physics terms. The 2005 prize recognised the frequency comb, which counts optical cycles, and the 2012 prize recognised quantum control of single trapped ions. Neither contains the magic-wavelength idea, in which a trapping potential is tuned so that it does not shift the clock transition, so Doppler and recoil effects vanish while thousands of atoms are interrogated in parallel. That is a distinct concept and it is what moved the field from the 10^-16 range to 10^-18. It is also not only a better number. At that level the atoms in the lattice are a controlled many-body system, with density, collisional and spin-exchange effects that had to be understood in physical detail, and clocks lifted by a millimetre visibly tick at a different rate. Independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, PTB, NIST, SYRTE) have reproduced and surpassed each other for roughly two decades and their comparisons agree. On the second question, I do not think a realised fundamental-physics result or the redefinition of the second is a precondition. We reward the demonstrated discovery, and 10^-18 performance with a stable interpretation is demonstrated; the citation should say so and should not lean on varying constants or dark matter, which are still limits. The credit is the cleanest on the shortlist: Katori proposed and first demonstrated the lattice clock, and Ye took it to the accuracy frontier.
statement.case_against: The honest weaknesses remain. First, some members will see a third clock-related prize after 2005 and 2012 and judge it a refinement of a recognised program. I have given my answer, but it is a judgement about what counts as a new regime, and Danielsson in particular has not been persuaded that a better ruler is a clue from nature. Second, priority is not perfectly captured by two names: Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Hinkley, Bloom and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE teams made decisive contributions, and trapped-ion clocks (Al+, Yb+) reached comparable accuracy by a different route, so the citation must be worded around the lattice scheme and not clocks in general. Third, I am a theorist in a neighbouring quantum-technology community and I rely on the clock community and external experts for the priority history; I have not verified the early lattice-clock record myself. Finally, B012 is attractive partly because it offends nobody, and I accept that consensus is not by itself a scientific argument; I support it because I find the physics case sufficient, not because of the support count.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B018, argues that the Z2 classification is a distinct step after the 2016 prize, and says he would accept B012 if topological matter fails to reach agreement.
responses.response: I agree with his physics: the quantum spin Hall edge transport has stood for two decades and is quantitatively understood, and the Z2 invariant is a real concept. My difficulty is the same one Eriksson and Danielsson raise, that the HgTe proposal of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is outside the trio and Zhang's death means that cannot be repaired. The 3D strand (Fu, Kane, Mele; Moore, Balents) cannot fit either. I would support B018 only if an external HgTe priority report made the Molenkamp part defensible. Without that, I keep it as my first alternative and I thank him for accepting B012 as the fallback, since that makes a joint outcome realistic.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B022, argues that flat bands and correlated insulators do not depend on the pairing mechanism, and notes that prizes have been awarded with mechanism questions open.
responses.response: That is a fair reply to my earlier remark and I accept the distinction: the existence of the flat bands and correlated states is settled, and a citation limited to them would not rest on pairing. Two problems remain for this year. Kroll points out that twist-angle disorder and device-to-device variability still limit reproducibility of the phase diagram, which matters to me as the criterion of robustness across laboratories. And the Cao omission cannot be resolved inside three names. I would put B022 in a prize in a few years and I regard it as the strongest condensed-matter alternative, but I do not think it is more mature than the clocks today. I also take his point about B064: the 2025 prize has reduced room for circuit QED, which is one reason I keep it out of my configuration.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers the experimental Higgs discovery (B055), says the 2013 prize honoured the mechanism and not the experimental observation, and names B012 as the configuration he could support most readily if individual attribution is judged indefensible.
responses.response: I defer to him on particle physics and agree that the 125 GeV boson is the larger discovery in the broad sense and that the 2013 prize does not discharge it. My objection is not to merit but to the allocation. His own file moved the trio to Gianotti, Jenni and Virdee, while Lindroth and the chair have named different names, and he concedes that Della Negra's claim is equally strong. A prize whose three names the committee cannot defend to the two collaborations would harm the award more than the clocks' lower profile does. I would ask whether he can say what an expert report would need to show for a three-name split to be defensible. If it cannot, his own condition points to B012.

responses.point: Olsson maintains B032 on merit as an original invention with a short list of originators, while acknowledging she is the only member ranking it high and that Knut Urban is omitted.
responses.response: I accept her correction that this is an invention that was demonstrated, reproduced and commercialised, and that the originator list is shorter than for the Higgs. I would still ask what the decisive discovery in physics is, as opposed to a very valuable instrument for other sciences, and the omission of Urban, who led the first corrected TEM with Haider and Rose, is a fairness problem that none of us can fix with three names. I note that her file names B012 as the most acceptable fallback and I would be glad to hear which conditions on the citation would make her comfortable. I also do not think our shared Chalmers affiliation affects either of our judgements here, since no shortlisted name is tied to either of us, but I note it.

responses.point: Kroll asks that the citation speak of the lattice-clock architecture and the 10^-18 regime, not of clocks in general, and treats the redefinition of the second as not decisive for timing.
responses.response: I agree on both points and I have changed my citation accordingly. My round-1 wording ended on opening new tests of fundamental physics; I removed that, because Pearce and Lindroth are right that those payoffs are still prospective and the results so far are limits. The new text names the magic-wavelength lattice and the 10^-18 regime and nothing more. I take Kroll's note about his year in Boulder as a disclosure and not a conflict, and I agree he need not recuse.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as a distinct achievement from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes; I have given my physical argument but it remains a judgement.
Whether an external expert report would confirm that Katori and Ye are the right two names, given Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto and the other lattice-clock groups.
Whether B018 could be rescued by an expert verdict on HgTe priority, which would change how I rank it as an alternative.

A two-part prize with a second achievement is not possible within three people, because B012 already uses two names and no other shortlisted achievement fits a single credited name; I therefore propose a single part.
My views on B055, B013 and B032 rely on colleagues' expertise outside my own field.
statement.conflict_note: I rank B064 (circuit QED) first in my opening ballot. I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology, work in the same superconducting-circuit community as the B064 candidates and the 2025 laureates, and have Chalmers colleagues in that area. I have kept B064 out of my configuration and out of my alternatives, and I would recuse from any discussion or vote on B064 or another superconducting-circuit candidate if it advanced. I have no tie to Katori, Ye, Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer that I know of, and no recusal need on B012, B018 or B022. Olsson is a Chalmers colleague, but no candidate is tied to either of us.
